etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English prince, from Anglo-Norman prince, from Latin prīnceps (“first head”), from prīmus (“first”) +‎ capiō (“seize, take”). Cognate with Old English fruma (“prince, ruler”). Doublet of princeps and principe.

Displaced native Middle English atheling, from Old English æþeling; Middle English kinebarn, from Old English cynebearn; Middle English alder, from Old English ealdor; and Middle English drighten, from Old English dryhten.

definitions.definition: (now archaic or historical) A (male) ruler, a sovereign; a king, monarch. [from 13th c.]

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, chapter 42, in John Florio, transl., The Essayes […], book I, London:  […]  Val[entine] Simmes for Edward Blount […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Truely, to see our Princes all alone, sitting at their meat, beleagred round with so many talkers, whisperers, and gazing beholders, unknowne what they are or whence they come, I have often rather pittied than envied them.

quote.citation: 2009, Diarmaid MacCulloch, A History of Christianity, Penguin, published 2010, page 600:
quote.text: By his last years Erasmus realized that princes like Henry VIII and François I had deceived him in their elaborate negotiations for universal peace, but his belief in the potential of princely power for good remained undimmed.

quote.citation: 2009, Hilary Mantel, Wolf Hall, Fourth Estate, published 2010, page 411:
quote.text: If Henry does not fully trust him, is it surprising? A prince is alone: in his council chamber, in his bedchamber, and finally in Hell's antechamber, stripped – as Harry Percy said – for Judgment.

quote.citation: 1605, M. N. [pseudonym; William Camden], Remaines of a Greater Worke, Concerning Britaine, […], London:  […]  G[eorge] E[ld] for Simon Waterson, →OCLC:
quote.text: Queen Elizabeth, a prince admirable above her sex.

definitions.definition: Someone who is preeminent in their field; a great person. [from 13th c.]
The (male) ruler or head of a principality. [from 14th c.]

quote.text: He is the prince who never grew up – a one-time playboy and son of the Hollywood star Grace Kelly and Prince Rainier of Monaco.

definitions.definition: A male member of a royal family other than the ruler; especially (in the United Kingdom) the son or grandson of the monarch. [from 14th c.]
A non-royal high title of nobility, especially in France and the Holy Roman Empire.

quote.text: Conspiracy theories are always enticing: one I was involved with in the 50s was about Mayerling, the 19th-century Austrian scandal involving a prince’s lover who died in dodgy circumstances in a hunting lodge.

definitions.definition: A type of court card used in tarot cards, the equivalent of the jack.
Any of various nymphalid butterflies of the genus Rohana.
(intransitive, rare, often followed by dummy subject it) To behave or act like a prince.

quote.citation: 1611 April (first recorded performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Cymbeline”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iii], page 382, column 1:
quote.text: The Roofes of Palaces, and Nature prompts them / In ſimple and lowe things, to Prince it, much / Beyond the tricke of others.

definitions.definition: (transitive, rare) To transform (someone) into a prince.

quote.citation: 2005 March 30, abe slaney, “Question re John Lennon's Death”, in rec.music.beatles‎[1] (Usenet):
quote.text: All I could remember is the chorus, and something about pumpkins turning into princesses (???!) and frogs turning into princes. I figured she meant the frog was John before she princed him.
